questions.stem: A newborn whose mother had poorly controlled diabetes is jittery a few hours after birth. The first concern is:

options.text: Hypoglycemia, because the baby made extra insulin and maternal glucose has now stopped
Hypocalcemia from a high parathyroid hormone

questions.explanation: Maternal glucose crossed the placenta; insulin did not. The baby made extra insulin and is at risk of low sugar after birth.

questions.stem: Which statement about pregnancy and insulin is correct?

options.text: Maternal insulin freely crosses the placenta and drives fetal growth
Only fetal glucose, not maternal glucose, reaches the baby
Maternal glucose crosses; maternal insulin does not

questions.explanation: The placenta lets glucose through and keeps maternal insulin out.

questions.stem: High blood calcium with a high, or unsuppressed, parathyroid hormone is:

options.text: A cancer peptide until proven otherwise

questions.explanation: The hormone should fall if the calcium is high for another reason. If it does not, the gland is driving the calcium.

questions.stem: High blood calcium with a suppressed parathyroid hormone points first to:

options.text: A parathyroid-independent cause, such as a cancer peptide

questions.explanation: When the hormone is appropriately low, look outside the gland.

questions.stem: High blood calcium, but the urine calcium is low. Next thought:

options.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is possible; do not operate on the blood number alone

questions.explanation: A low urine calcium can be familial. Surgery is not decided from the blood calcium alone.

questions.stem: A low-dose suppression test fails. What has been shown?

options.text: The source is definitely the pituitary
Cortisol is not under normal control; the organ has not been named
The source is definitely the adrenal

questions.explanation: Every Cushing syndrome can fail the low-dose test. That finding does not name the organ.

questions.stem: A high-dose suppression test can suppress cortisol when the source is:
questions.explanation: A high-dose test can still suppress a pituitary source. Adrenal and ectopic sources usually do not suppress.

questions.stem: A low driving hormone (adrenocorticotropic hormone) with high cortisol points to:
questions.explanation: If the driving hormone is already low, the gland itself is making the cortisol.

options.text: It only converts T4 to T3 in the tissues
It organifies iodide and couples tyrosines
It crosses the placenta in place of insulin

questions.explanation: The enzyme organifies iodide and couples tyrosines in the gland.

questions.stem: Which thionamide also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3?
questions.explanation: Common thionamides block the enzyme; propylthiouracil also blocks peripheral conversion.
